action_criteria.rationale: The outside report of enlarged ventricles needs measurement of the markers, a search for infarcts or microbleeds given her AF, and exclusion of an obstructing lesion.

action_criteria.rationale: Removing 40 mL with normal opening pressure and normal CSF content tests whether her gait improves when CSF is drained.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not perform the large-volume lumbar tap before brain MRI has excluded a mass or obstructive hydrocephalus

Do not diagnose iNPH from ventriculomegaly alone: the diagnosis needs the clinical syndrome (gait disturbance with cognitive or urinary symptoms) and supportive imaging, with no other cause explaining them [Relkin_2005]
Do not perform the lumbar tap while apixaban is active and do not bridge with heparin [ASRA_2025] [ACCP_2022]
Do not attribute the gait and cognitive decline to cardioembolic or small-vessel disease from atrial fibrillation when the MRI shows no infarcts and only Fazekas 1 change
required_recommendations: Refer to neurosurgery for CSF shunting with a programmable valve, on the basis of the tap-test improvement of 33% in TUG at 24 hours, the DESH MRI and normal-pressure CSF [Nakajima_2021]

Hold apixaban for at least 72 hours before the lumbar tap and restart it no sooner than 24 hours after, without heparin bridging, weighing the interruption against the stroke risk of atrial fibrillation (CHA2DS2-VASc 4) [ASRA_2025] [ACCP_2022]
Falls-prevention measures (physiotherapy, home assessment, walking aid) while awaiting surgery

avoided_actions.rationale: She has had no seizures or fluctuating awareness, so an EEG does not address her progressive gait and cognitive syndrome.
Her paroxysmal AF is already diagnosed and treated, and her falls are gait falls without syncope, so an ECG adds nothing to the work-up.
Her AF is already anticoagulated, so an echocardiogram changes neither the iNPH work-up nor her stroke prevention.
MRI is available and measures the callosal angle, DESH and hippocampi and shows microbleeds that CT cannot.
Her paroxysmal AF was diagnosed on a Holter 14 months ago and is anticoagulated, so repeat rhythm monitoring has no diagnostic role here.
Molecular or advanced imaging does not change the iNPH decision, which rests on MRI and the tap test.
A full neuropsychological battery is not needed for the iNPH decision; the bedside screen and timed gait measures are.
A 2.5-year course without rapid decline, fever or inflammatory features gives no indication for prion, inflammatory or infectious CSF assays.

differential.diagnosis: Vascular cognitive impairment / small-vessel or cardioembolic ischaemic disease
differential.key_features: AF and hypertension are vascular risks, but the MRI shows Fazekas 1 change without infarcts or microhaemorrhages, and her gait improves after CSF removal.
Freezing at doorways overlaps, but there is no tremor or rigidity and the wide-based gait improves after the tap.
Her mother had Alzheimer's disease, but gait came first, recall improves with cueing, MTA is 2 (within the range for age 77) and the MoCA rises after the tap.

differential.diagnosis: Cerebral atrophy with secondary ex-vacuo ventriculomegaly
differential.key_features: Ventricles disproportionate to cortical volume loss, tight high-convexity sulci and an acute callosal angle argue against ex-vacuo enlargement.

differential.diagnosis: Secondary (post-traumatic, post-haemorrhagic or post-meningitic) communicating hydrocephalus
differential.key_features: There is no history of head injury, haemorrhage or meningitis before the gait decline, and SWI shows no siderosis or subdural collection.

key_clinical_evidence: Probable iNPH requires an insidious gait disturbance after age 40, progressing over at least 3 to 6 months without an antecedent cause, plus cognitive or urinary symptoms; she has all three over 2.5 years [Relkin_2005]
MRI shows Evans index 0.39 with both DESH components, a callosal angle of 74 degrees and temporal horn enlargement, with no obstructing lesion, infarcts or microhaemorrhages [Relkin_2005]
Opening pressure 14 cmH2O with normal CSF content meets the pressure criterion [Relkin_2005]

After removal of 40 mL, TUG fell from 30 to 20 s (33%) at 24 hours and the 10-m walk from 24 to 16 s; an improvement of 10% or more in TUG is a commonly used positive threshold, though no guideline sets a single cut-off
Apixaban is held for at least 72 hours before a neuraxial puncture and restarted no sooner than 24 hours after, without heparin bridging [ASRA_2025] [ACCP_2022]
The tap test has a sensitivity of 26% to 61% and a PPV of 73% to 100%, so a clear response supports shunting while a negative tap would not have excluded it [Marmarou_2005]

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Atrial fibrillation does not produce ventriculomegaly with DESH or a gait that improves after CSF removal, and the MRI shows no infarcts; it changes the anticoagulant plan around the tap, not the diagnosis.
red_herrings.data_point: Known paroxysmal atrial fibrillation on apixaban
red_herrings.intended_effect: Invites a vascular or cardioembolic explanation for the gait and cognitive decline, deferring the tap test and the shunt question

sequence_constraints.reason: Brain imaging must exclude a mass or obstructive hydrocephalus before CSF is removed [Relkin_2005]
The baseline gait must be measured before the tap, or the post-tap change cannot be interpreted [Nakajima_2021]
The timed gait is repeated after the tap, at 2 to 24 hours, so that its change from the baseline measures the response to CSF removal [Nakajima_2021]

patient.history_present_illness: A 77-year-old retired interior designer with paroxysmal atrial fibrillation (on apixaban), hypertension, and hyperlipidemia was admitted for evaluation of progressive gait, bladder and memory decline. Her son and daughter-in-law prompted the admission. She has had progressive gait difficulty over the past 2.5 years, starting with an insidious change in step length and gait speed. She now has a distinctive wide-based shuffling walk and has had six falls while walking or turning in the past 18 months, none with loss of consciousness or palpitations, including one serious fall that required emergency department evaluation for possible hip fracture (X-rays negative). She now uses a cane indoors and a rollator walker outdoors. Her urinary urgency began approximately 20 months ago, progressing from urgency without leakage to daily leakage. She rarely leaves home without wearing protective undergarments. Her cognitive decline has been notable: she can no longer manage her finances (her son has taken over), she repeats questions frequently within the same conversation, and she has twice gotten confused while walking in her own apartment building. She has been taking apixaban for 14 months for paroxysmal AF diagnosed on a Holter monitor. A brain MRI obtained two months ago at an outside facility was reported as showing enlarged ventricles; the images are not available. Her primary care physician referred her for progressive gait difficulty with memory decline and urinary incontinence.
